title: Biosynthesis of Heme and Porphyrias
objectives: Compare erythroid and hepatic regulation of heme synthesis
Classify porphyrias based on enzyme defects
Explain clinical management of porphyric attacks

heme_structure.title: Heme Structure & Function
heme_structure.content:
Heme Characteristics

Composition: Porphyrin ring + Fe2+ with side chains (acetyl, methyl, propionyl, vinyl)

  • Functions: Oxygen transport (Hb/Mb), electron transport (cytochromes), enzymatic reactions (catalase, NO synthase)
  • Properties: Soret band absorption (400nm), red fluorescence under UV light

biosynthesis.title: Heme Biosynthesis Pathway
biosynthesis.content:
8-Step Biosynthesis

1. ALA Formation (Mitochondria)

  • Glycine + succinyl-CoA → δ-aminolevulinate (ALA)
  • Catalyzed by ALA synthase (PLP-dependent)
  • Commited step with 2 isozymes: ALAS-1 (liver), ALAS-2 (erythroid)

2. Porphobilinogen (Cytosol)

  • 2 ALA → porphobilinogen (ALA dehydratase, Zn2+-dependent)
  • Lead target: Inhibits this step

3. Hydroxymethylbilane (Cytosol)

  • 4 porphobilinogen → linear tetrapyrrole (hydroxymethylbilane synthase)

4. Uroporphyrinogen III (Cytosol)

  • Cyclization/isomerization (uroporphyrinogen III synthase)
  • Deficiency: Spontaneous formation of non-physiological type I isomer

5. Coproporphyrinogen III (Cytosol)

  • Decarboxylation of acetyl groups → methyl (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase)

6. Protoporphyrinogen III (Mitochondria)

  • Oxidative decarboxylation of propionyl groups → vinyl (coproporphyrinogen oxidase, O2-dependent)

7. Protoporphyrin IX (Mitochondria)

  • Oxidation of protoporphyrinogen (protoporphyrinogen oxidase)

8. Heme Formation (Mitochondria)

  • Fe2+ incorporation (ferrochelatase)
  • Lead target: Also inhibits this final step

regulation.title: Regulation of Heme Synthesis
regulation.content:
Tissue-Specific Control

Erythroid Cells

  • ALAS-2 controlled by iron availability
  • Hemin feedback inhibition when heme accumulates
  • X-linked sideroblastic anemia: ALAS-2 mutations

Hepatocytes

  • ALAS-1 repressed by heme (reduces synthesis & mitochondrial import)
  • Induced by CYP450-inducing drugs (barbiturates, alcohol)
  • Hemin (Fe3+ heme) increases mRNA degradation

porphyrias.title: Porphyrias Classification
porphyrias.content:
Porphyria Disorders

General Features

  • Red-blue urine (porphyrin pigments)
  • Autosomal dominant (mostly)
  • Two pathological mechanisms:
    1. Neurovisceral symptoms (pre-ring closure defects)
    2. Photosensitivity (post-ring closure defects)

Erythropoietic Porphyrias

  • Congenital Erythropoietic: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency
  • Protoporphyria: Ferrochelatase deficiency
  • Both cause severe photosensitivity

Acute Hepatic Porphyrias

  • Acute Intermittent: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase deficiency (↑ALA/PBG)
  • Precipitated by CYP-inducers (barbiturates)
  • Neuropsychiatric symptoms (anxiety → delirium)

Chronic Hepatic Porphyria

  • Porphyria Cutanea Tarda: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency
  • Precipitated by iron, alcohol, estrogens, hepatitis
  • Late-onset cutaneous lesions

Acquired Porphyria

  • Lead Poisoning: Inhibits ALA dehydratase & ferrochelatase
  • ↑Urinary ALA & RBC protoporphyrins

management.title: Clinical Management
management.content:
Therapeutic Approaches

Acute Attacks

  • IV hemin (suppresses ALAS-1)
  • High-dose glucose (represses ALAS-1)
  • Symptom control (pain/nausea)

Chronic Management

  • Photosensitivity: Sunscreen, antioxidants
  • Porphyria Cutanea Tarda: Phlebotomy (reduce iron)
  • Avoid precipitating drugs/alcohol

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why do pre-ring closure defects cause neurological symptoms? +

A: Accumulated ALA/PBG are neurotoxic, causing vasoconstriction and autonomic dysfunction that manifests as abdominal pain, psychiatric symptoms, and motor neuropathy.

Q: How does lead poisoning mimic porphyria? +

A: Lead inhibits both ALA dehydratase (early) and ferrochelatase (late), causing ALA accumulation and RBC protoporphyrin elevation - similar to genetic porphyrias but without photosensitivity.

Q: Why does glucose infusion help acute porphyric attacks? +

A> Glucose represses ALAS-1 transcription in hepatocytes, reducing accumulation of toxic precursors during crises when heme synthesis is blocked.
